sentences.t: Revenue rose 26% on the year to $64.6 billion in the September quarter, a record.

Reported operating income was $12.99 billion after a $9.89 billion charge for Meta's settlement with US state attorneys general over teen mental health on its platforms; excluding it, operating income would have been $22.88 billion and diluted EPS $7.40 instead of the reported $3.83.

Capital expenditure including finance leases was $34.91 billion in the quarter, and Meta narrowed its full-year capex outlook to $135-145 billion from $130-145 billion - the narrowed range raises the floor $5 billion from July's.
Fourth-quarter revenue is guided to $73-76 billion.

The board also declared a one-time stock dividend of one share of a new Class C stock for each outstanding Class A and Class B share, contingent on an amended and restated charter taking effect 19 January 2027, with record and payment dates still to be set; Meta says it expects the Class A price to reflect the effect of a two-for-one split once paid, that the dividend changes no shareholder's voting power, and that the amended charter was approved by shareholder written consent.
Shares initially rose more than 4% in after-hours trading before settling to a gain of about 2%.

The same Wednesday, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company liable over Facebook's user-data practices tied to the Cambridge Analytica era, with the judge writing that the company's wrongdoing went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices"; Meta said it intends to appeal (AP, BBC).
Why it matters to you: the AI capex race is the demand engine under your IT stocks and the Nasdaq alike - Meta at up to $145 billion a year is a floor under that trade.
The penalty is the counter-story: the bill for the last decade's data practices is still arriving while this decade's build-out accelerates.

Editor's takeaway: record revenue and a $5 billion higher capex floor say the build-out is still accelerating; the $25 billion penalty says the bill for the last decade's data practices is still arriving.
Both land on the same balance sheet.
Eternal - the parent of Zomato and Blinkit - reported September-quarter profit of ₹125 crore, up 92% on the year, against a CNBC-TV18 poll estimate of ₹250 crore.
Revenue rose 77.6% to ₹24,138 crore, ahead of the poll's ₹22,425 crore, and EBITDA of ₹752 crore beat the ₹530 crore estimate, a 3.1% margin against 2.4% expected.
Expenses rose 75% to ₹24,166 crore.
The results landed after the closing bell; the stock had already closed down 2.45% at ₹312.35 (NSE) before they were public.
Why it matters to you: the street's complaint is profitability pace, not demand - revenue and EBITDA beat while the profit line missed on costs.
That is the same tension the quick-commerce build-out has carried for six quarters, and it decides how patient the market stays with every consumer-internet name on your watchlist.
Editor's takeaway: a 92% profit rise that disappoints tells you how much expectation is already in the price.
The Nifty opened 127 points up at 23,016 on Wednesday, tracking an overnight AI-led rally on Wall Street, and touched 23,120 within twenty minutes.
That was the day's high.
Selling pulled it below 22,700 by early afternoon, to a low near 22,650, before a closing recovery left it at 22,811.35, down 77.60 points (0.34%).
The Sensex closed at 73,709.69, down 143.21 points (0.19%), and Bank Nifty fell 0.92% to 54,976.90 (NSE closing data via AlphaTribe and The Hindu BusinessLine).
Beneath the index the day was worse.
Decliners beat advancers 2,036 to 291; only 13.7% of Nifty 500 stocks sit above their 50-day averages; 51 stocks hit 52-week lows against two new highs.
IT was the only green sector, up 2.88%, while chemicals fell 2.64%.

Options-implied volatility rose from 12.6% to 14.2%, and foreign investors remain positioned heavily bearish in index futures - 9.5% long against 84% for retail and HNI accounts (Zerodha Aftermarket Report, 21 Oct).
The flows disagreed with the tape.
Foreign investors were net buyers of ₹1,022.30 crore in the cash market and domestic institutions bought ₹1,614.30 crore (NSE/BSE provisional figures via 5paisa's daily table).

The rupee gained 46 paise to close at 94.45 per dollar, its strongest close since 4 September, helped by optimism over an India-US trade deal and foreign inflows toward the Jio IPO (Aftermarket Report).

US markets that night continued the AI bid: the Nasdaq rose 1.05% to 26,702.86, the S&P 500 0.58% to 7,757.17 and the Dow 0.69% to 52,856.09; SpaceX jumped 7.8% on its first profit as a public company and Super Micro 9.6% (Reuters/AP wrap).
Overnight earnings added two more data points to the AI ledger.

Tesla's third-quarter revenue was roughly flat at $28.05 billion while GAAP net income fell to $787 million from $1.37 billion a year earlier; free cash flow was $1.53 billion and the company says Optimus production has begun at Fremont - a vendor claim, dated (Tesla's 8-K filing via stocktitan).
IBM's revenue rose 5% to $17.1 billion with software up 8%; it expects full-year free cash flow up more than $1 billion versus 2025 and constant-currency revenue growth of 4-5% (IBM's press release).
Both stocks rose modestly after hours.

The split personality of the day - heavy breadth, positive institutional flows, a firming rupee - is what a market looks like when index-level selling is concentrated in rate-sensitives rather than broad risk.
HDFC Bank found that two senior executives leaked confidential business information to outsiders, an internal probe has revealed, according to NDTV reporting from Wednesday.
The review is ongoing and will determine whether the leaked information was misused.
For India's largest private bank - usually the sector's governance reference point - the question now is what the information was and who used it.

Why it matters to you: if your work touches bancassurance or bank partnerships, governance headlines at the anchor bank move partner conversations and compliance checklists; watch for the probe's findings and any exchange disclosure.

Bajaj Finance reported a strong quarter - net interest income up 23.6% to ₹13,335 crore, profit up 28.7% to ₹6,367 crore, and it raised FY27 AUM growth guidance - yet the stock fell 3.27% Wednesday because of what management said next: margin compression could exceed the guided 10-15 basis points in the second half as the RBI's repo hike works through funding costs, after roughly 5 basis points of compression already in the first half.

Why it matters to you: this is the transmission channel from the lead story into earnings - when the RBI moves the repo rate, NBFC funding costs reprice faster than loan books, and the largest, best-funded NBFC is saying even it cannot fully dodge the squeeze.
Every lender on your watchlist gets asked the Bajaj question on its next call.

India's Index of Core Industries rose 7.9% on the year in September, up from a revised 5.9% in August, on coal up 10.7%, iron ore up 18.4% and refinery products up 10.3% (commerce ministry release; Mint; TOI).
The print supports the RBI's decision to upgrade FY27 growth to 7.1% - the economy was accelerating into the oil shock.
Zetwerk lists tomorrow - and its prospectus holds the week's best diligence lesson.

The offer for sale shows what each seller paid for its shares: founders Amrit Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan sell 14.23 million shares each at a "negligible" acquisition cost (about ₹215 crore each at the cap); seed fund Kae Capital exits part at ₹3.94 a share (38 times its cost at the ₹151 cap); Peak XV's Investments V fund at ₹6.31.
One promoter-group entity, Creovate Innovation - a company both founders also direct - sells shares it acquired at ₹178.58, above the ₹151 price-band cap: an underwater exit in the same document.
The long read tells the full story.

The insight: Accel's Prayank Swaroop passed the classic diligence test in December 2018 - experts called Zetwerk a "vitamin" (nice to have), customers called it a "painkiller" (they could not ship without it) - and the customers were right.
But the mechanism that made it scale was not the marketplace; it was the second pivot, to owning execution risk as the supplier of record.
Marketplaces match; businesses that bear the risk get the margin.

Opportunities this creates: managed-marketplace models are now proven in custom manufacturing; the same "supplier of record" wrapper is open in fragmented Indian categories with execution gaps - industrial maintenance, contract packaging, testing-and-certification labs.
One startup idea: an RHP-reading service for retail IPO investors.
Every prospectus already discloses each selling shareholder's acquisition cost - almost nobody reads it.

A tool that turns the OFS table into a one-page "who sells at what multiple" card (flagging underwater sellers like Creovate) sells to brokerages and wealth apps as an engagement feature; the data is free, the moat is parsing accuracy across thousands of filings.

OpenAI's models are coming to Google Cloud's Vertex AI model garden, announced by both companies on 21 October: select customers get limited-preview access now, with general availability planned in the coming weeks (OpenAI's announcement).
Google says this makes it the only hyperscaler offering all three leading closed model families - its claim, dated 21 October, and worth treating as vendor framing until independently checked.

The substance underneath the framing: enterprise buyers increasingly refuse single-model lock-in, and OpenAI - which competes with Google on models and consumer AI - now rents shelf space on Google's enterprise rails.

Why it matters to you: if your product or team builds on any single model API, this is the market telling you multi-model is becoming the default enterprise posture - procurement will expect it, and routing between vendors is turning into a standard architecture decision rather than an exotic one.
Radar, last 24-48 hours: Meta narrowed its 2026 capex outlook to $135-145 billion while posting a record quarter (above).
"BAND" launched on Product Hunt - a shared chat layer for coordinating multiple AI agents and human teams with governance controls; single-source, vendor-described, listed 21 October.
SpaceX reported its first profit as a public company, sending the stock up 7.8% (Reuters; Washington Post).
Tesla and SpaceX have each formed special board committees to weigh a potential merger, Musk said (CNBC, TechCrunch, 20-21 October).
Nothing else verified in the window worth your attention.

The build-relevant note in the OpenAI-Google news: Vertex AI's model garden means that once general availability lands in the coming weeks, one Google Cloud project will call Gemini, Anthropic and OpenAI models behind a single IAM and billing surface.
If you prototype multi-model routing, that consolidation removes the messiest part - separate credentials and quotas per vendor.
A router that sends extraction jobs to the cheapest adequate model and escalates hard ones becomes an afternoon's work once every model sits behind one endpoint.
Build an OFS cost-basis card for one IPO (about 30 minutes).
Open the Zetwerk RHP (linked in the IPO section) and copy the offer-for-sale table - seller, shares offered, acquisition cost.
Paste it into your AI tool of choice with: "Turn this table into a one-page card.
For each seller show shares sold, cost per share, and the multiple earned at the ₹151 cap price.

Flag any seller exiting below cost." A good result names Creovate Innovation as the underwater seller without being told, computes Kae Capital's 38x and the founders' ~₹215 crore each, and shows its arithmetic.
You will have built the startup idea from the startup section, in miniature, in half an hour.

In 1967 the Yale economist William Brainard proved something that became central banking's folk wisdom: when you are unsure what your policy actually does, do less of it - the "attenuation principle".
Alan Blinder's 1998 book carried it to a generation of central bankers, and Blinder himself suspected it was "more wise in the real world than the mathematics will support".

In August 2023, three Banque de France economists - Stéphane Dupraz, Sophie Guilloux-Nefussi and Adrian Penalver - published the catch in the International Journal of Central Banking ("A Pitfall of Cautiousness in Monetary Policy", Vol 19, No 3).

Their model shows that for a central bank, caution has a hidden cost the textbook misses: moving less is only safe if the public's inflation expectations stay put, but the very act of moving less tells firms and households the bank is not serious - expectations drift away from target, and the bank ends up tightening as much as it was reluctant to, for a worse outcome.
The authors are careful about limits: they do not claim uncertainty never justifies caution, only that central banks carry a systematic bias toward being too cautious.
You watched the concept run live on Wednesday.

In the RBI's October minutes, executive director Indranil Bhattacharyya argues it is better to "set aside the cautiousness bias and act in a pre-emptive manner" than to wait and watch - better a small hike today than a forced large one after expectations unhinge - and the minutes' footnote for that phrase cites the Dupraz-Guilloux-Nefussi-Penalver paper above directly.

Read through this edition's lens - an editorial interpretation, since the members do not mention Brainard - the two dissenters, Nagesh Kumar and Ram Singh, voted the Brainard side of the argument: uncertain about transmission, so attenuate.
The 4-2 vote on the stance is, almost literally, the paper's two positions meeting a real decision.
The applications run past central banks.

In insurance distribution, the same bias appears when an advisor delays a hard renewal-conversation because the outcome is uncertain - the client's expectation of "same as last year" hardens with every quiet week, and the eventual correction costs more trust than an early one would have.
In product work, shipping a hesitant half-fix signals that the problem is tolerable, and users build habits around it.
The paper's escape route is commitment: pre-announce the trigger you will act on, and hesitation stops moving anyone's expectations.
The decision rule: when your audience's expectations move in response to your delay, hesitation is not free - price the drift.
Act early and small, or pre-commit to a trigger; do not wait for certainty that arrives only after expectations have moved.
Sixty-second recall: close the page and answer: (1) What does Brainard's attenuation principle say?
(2) Why does it backfire for a central bank specifically?
(3) Which RBI member cited this research on Wednesday, and on which side?
(4) The decision rule, in one sentence.
Answers: (1) When uncertain about your policy's effects, do less.
(2) Because the public reads hesitation as unseriousness and inflation expectations drift - forcing the bank to do as much later for a worse outcome.
(3) Executive director Indranil Bhattacharyya, arguing to act pre-emptively.
(4) When your delay moves others' expectations, act early and small or pre-commit to a trigger.
The part of an IPO where existing shareholders sell their own shares and pocket the money themselves - unlike a fresh issue, where the company sells new shares and keeps the proceeds.
Zetwerk's ₹5,012 crore issue mixes both: ₹2,830 crore fresh (to the company) and about ₹2,182 crore OFS (to founders and investors selling).
The split tells you who the listing is for; the OFS table tells you what each seller originally paid.
What I think the market is missing - an analytical read, not advice.
The equity market heard the unanimous hike and sold rate-sensitives; the bond market did the cleaner reading of the split, taking the 10-year to 7.44% - its highest since November 2022.
I think the 4-2 stance split matters more than the unanimous hike, because the dissenters' "neutral" is where the pause case now lives, and December is six weeks away.

My falsifiable marker: if this reading is right, Bank Nifty keeps underperforming the Nifty while the 10-year holds above roughly 7.4%, and Bajaj Finance's margin warning stops looking company-specific.
Wrong if the yield slips back under about 7.3% on its own, or if Thursday's trade treats the minutes as old news and rate-sensitives lead a rebound.

Scoreboard on yesterday's calls: the Brewing note said the minutes could reveal a split - no credit there: the 4-2 stance split was already public in the 7 October resolution, which named Kumar and Singh; the minutes added the reasoning, not the split.

The editor's watch list had crude staying high (yes, Brent settled at $108.82), IT responding to the US tech rebound (yes, +2.88%, the only green sector), and foreign selling extending (no - FIIs turned net buyers of ₹1,022 crore on the exchange-provisional basis).
Two of three.
Zetwerk lists Friday against a grey premium that faded from ₹14 to ₹3.50 - the open tests whether subscription multiples or grey pricing lied.
Watch the first-hour open versus the ₹151 cap.
Wrong if the grey premium revives above ₹20 before listing or the open is a non-event within 2% of the cap.
IRDAI comments close Sunday 25 October: the distribution-economics consultation paper - and its transition glide path - reprices agent economics and bancassurance income lines.
Wrong if the regulator extends the window or signals a materially longer phase-in before Sunday.
The 2-4 December MPC is now a live meeting with a known fault line: Kumar and Singh on record for neutral.
Watch the October CPI print on 12 November and crude; two more high readings isolate the dissenters.
Wrong if inflation undershoots the RBI's 6.0% Q3 track and the stance question goes quiet.
Today, Thu 22 Oct: results from Swiggy, Havells, HPCL, Colgate-Palmolive India, Cyient, CreditAccess Grameen, Adani Energy Solutions, Adani Total Gas (exchange filings via TotalMarket).

Fri 23 Oct: Zetwerk, Tonbo Imaging and Bonfiglioli Transmissions list (investorgain); Jio IPO closes (chittorgarh); results from Infosys, Dr Reddy's, IndusInd Bank, JSW Steel, Adani Power, BPCL, Coforge; ex-dates for Tech Mahindra, ICICI Lombard and six others (NSE notices via TotalMarket).
Sat 24 Oct: results from Kotak Mahindra Bank, IDFC First Bank, AU Small Finance Bank, Castrol India (TotalMarket results calendar).
Sun 25 Oct: public comments close on IRDAI's distribution-economics consultation paper (IRDAI).
Mon 26 Oct: Jio Platforms IPO allotment expected (investorgain).
Tue 27 Oct: LTTS ₹20 dividend goes ex (TotalMarket); October F&O series expires (Aftermarket Report).
Wed 28 Oct: Jio Platforms lists on BSE and NSE (chittorgarh).

X was not accessed for this edition; the radar was verified through official posts (OpenAI, Google Cloud, Meta, IBM), a filing mirror (stocktitan) and Product Hunt, with vendor claims dated and labelled.
Discovery layer: Zerodha Pulse and DayStarter were used as pointers only; Pulse surfaced the Meta penalty and HDFC Bank items, both traced to AP/BBC and NDTV respectively.
Zerodha's Aftermarket Report (21 Oct issue, read in full) supplied session detail, positioning data and the 10-year yield; its figures are dated and labelled in-line.

New sources in use this edition: AlphaTribe (NSE closing movers snapshot), TotalMarket (corporate-actions board compiled from NSE notices), 5paisa (daily FII/DII provisional table), investorgain (live IPO grey-market table), the International Journal of Central Banking (primary research for today's concept), AP and BBC (Meta penalty), NDTV (HDFC Bank).
Two content-farm sites (wittytrades, chinimandi) surfaced in searches and were rejected.
India VIX and the NSDL basis of FII flows were dropped: no clean second source for the VIX close, and the NSDL figure measures a different flow basis than the exchange provisional data printed above.
Markets are watchlist-only.
Nothing here is a tip, a target or a buy/sell call.
Edition 17.
The long read: "The marketplace that learned to hold the wrench" - Zetwerk's road from a one-room Bengaluru office to tomorrow's listing bell.
Towards the end of 2017, Amrit Acharya had a problem that looked nothing like a problem.
He was an IIT Madras graduate with four years at ITC, a Berkeley MBA and a high-paying job at McKinsey in San Francisco.
Two things wore him down.
The advisory life meant, as he later put it, "you never knew what was going to happen to that advice".
And his US visa situation had gone bad enough that his firm suggested a migratory arrangement - six months in Australia, then maybe six months somewhere new.
When the second rotation came up, he snapped.
His girlfriend, now his wife, settled it: "Uncertainty is not a bad thing necessarily." They flew home in January 2018.
His father was less lyrical.
"I don't want to introduce you as my unemployed son to any of my relatives," he told Acharya, and gave him a deadline: figure out the next move before the wedding.
So in May 2018, with three IIT friends - Srinath Ramakkrushnan, Vishal Chaudhary and Rahul Sharma - Acharya started Zetwerk.
The plan was B2B software: tools to help companies manage their supply chains.
Within a month they had a $1.5 million seed term sheet from Kae Capital and Sequoia.
Then, in June 2018 - before a rupee of that seed money had reached the bank - they pivoted.
The software would become a marketplace instead: a place where companies could discover custom-manufacturing suppliers.
Acharya had to call investors who had signed for a SaaS company and tell them it was now a different business.
"We were worried.
We did not know how they would react," he recalled to Forbes India.
Both stayed.
It was the first of two escapes that made the company.
The marketplace ran into a human problem immediately.
Zetwerk's suppliers were small and mid-sized factories - many in places like Chhattisgarh - and to them a new customer was not an opportunity; it was a risk.
Would this unknown Bengaluru company pay on time?
Were there hidden terms?
"You Google us, and you would see nothing," Acharya said of the one-room-office days.
The founders spent months convincing factory owners that the order on the screen was real money.
In December 2018, Accel's Prayank Swaroop was circling a $9 million investment and doing his calls.
The B2B experts he phoned were nearly unanimous: Zetwerk would stay a small business - a "vitamin", nice to have.
Then he called the customers.
They described something else: a "painkiller" they could not ship without.
"That was the moment of truth for me," Swaroop said.
Accel's term sheet was ready in under ten days.
The diligence lesson outlived the deal: experts price categories, customers price pain.
But the customers' pain turned out to be deeper than discovery.
Suppliers found on the platform missed deadlines - for capacity reasons, financing reasons, logistics reasons.
A pure marketplace could introduce buyer and factory; it could not make the factory deliver.
So Zetwerk pivoted a second time, and this one was the real company: it became the supplier of record.
A customer orders from Zetwerk; Zetwerk owes the delivery; behind the curtain, it splits the order across multiple small factories running in parallel - "parallel manufacturing", Swaroop called it.
The marketplace had learned to hold the wrench.

They got plenty wrong along the way, and Acharya admits the biggest self-inflicted one: "We got very experienced senior folks too early in our journey." The perfectionist veterans and the break-things young engineers never fused.
Half the company's early life also ran through Covid lockdowns - Zetwerk went remote-first, and Acharya has said he never met over half his own employees.
None of it shows in the unicorn headlines; all of it is in the prospectus's risk factors, which still warn that its third-party suppliers can fail on capacity, quality and components.
The growth was real.
Revenue went from ₹21 crore in FY19 to ₹949 crore in FY21.
In August 2021, D1 Capital Partners led a $150 million Series E at a $1.33 billion valuation - by Forbes India's count the country's 26th unicorn of that year, in three years flat.
Acharya insisted the tag he valued was different: Zetwerk was a profitable unicorn, which meant "the velocity of growth" would be sustainable and fundraising would stay "a choice in my hands".
Then the story left the script.
The RHP filed this October shows revenue from operations of ₹12,364 crore in FY24 - and ₹11,332 crore in FY25.
A decline, in the middle of the blitzscale years, in the year the IPO was being prepared.
FY26 recovered to ₹15,913 crore.
The bottom line needs care, because the filing carries it on three tracks.

Losses from continuing operations ran ₹852 crore in FY24, narrowed to ₹215 crore in FY25 and widened again to ₹964 crore in FY26; adding the civil-infrastructure business the company chose to discontinue takes total restated losses to ₹918 crore, ₹371 crore and ₹1,606 crore across the three years.

Underneath both tracks the operating trend is genuinely better: the continuing-operations loss before exceptional items and tax fell from ₹427 crore in FY24 to ₹81 crore in FY26, and adjusted EBITDA reached ₹421 crore in FY26.
The headline losses are swollen by one-offs - FY26's ₹836 crore of exceptional items were primarily a non-cash charge for adjusting the conversion ratios on its share classes.

The latest June quarter shows the same pattern: the continuing-operations loss was ₹64 crore against ₹881 crore a year earlier, while the total loss including the discontinued civil-infrastructure business was ₹733 crore against ₹1,368 crore - ₹669 crore of this year's from the business being wound down.
The continuing track's narrowing says less about suddenly found religion than about the one-offs falling away.
The market had already said so once, privately.
A $210 million Series F in December 2021, led by Greenoaks Capital, marked the company at $2.7 billion (Mint).
Two years later, in October 2023, Zetwerk raised $120 million more at a flat valuation, Avenir Growth leading at ₹407.4 a share (entrackr) - flat, with the FY25 revenue decline still ahead of it.
Close to $90 million raised across 2024 in installments, led by Khosla Ventures, nudged the mark to $3.1 billion (The Hindu BusinessLine).
The IPO's ₹151 cap values the company at about ₹25,583 crore, roughly $2.7 billion (Mint) - level with the December 2021 dollar mark.

The cleaner comparator is the share price in rupees: the April and July 2026 private placements closed at ₹171 per equity share on the RHP’s own conversion-adjusted basis, so the ₹151 offer cap prices about 12% below those placements.
Note also that ₹407.4 and ₹151 are not clean comparisons: the exceptional charges above were primarily the adjustment of conversion ratios between share classes.
The founders' answer to the stall was to grow into the question: FY26 revenue rebounded 40%, and the IPO followed.
Which brings us to Friday morning.

The issue - ₹2,830 crore of fresh shares for the company and an offer for sale of 144.5 million shares by existing holders, about ₹2,182 crore at the ₹151 cap - closed Monday subscribed 3.06 times - institutions at 4.73 times and non-institutional buyers at 1.40, while retail stopped at 73 per cent, the same caution Jio's retail book showed on day one (PTI).

The anchor book had already committed ₹2,251 crore at ₹151: BlackRock, Goldman Sachs, Nomura, Capital Group, Norway's Government Pension Fund Global and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority among 99 funds (PTI).
Respectable and unspectacular, next to the 136 times that defence-imaging firm Tonbo drew the same week.
Zetwerk's unofficial grey-market premium faded from ₹14 on 15 October to ₹3.50 by 19 October, with none recorded at the last update.
The document's seller table is the quietest drama in it.
The two promoter-founders, Acharya and Ramakkrushnan, sell 14.23 million shares each - about ₹215 crore each at the cap - against an acquisition cost the RHP records as "negligible".
Kae Capital, the seed investor who heard about the first pivot by phone, sells shares that cost ₹3.94 for a 38-times return.
Peak XV's Investments V fund paid ₹6.31 a share.
And one promoter-group entity, Creovate Innovation - which both founders also direct - sells shares acquired at ₹178.58 apiece, above the cap price: an underwater exit printed in black and white.

The other two founders from the May 2018 photograph, Vishal Chaudhary and Rahul Sharma, are in the table as well, selling up to 1.71 million shares each - about ₹26 crore apiece at the cap - and CFO Ankit Fatehpuria - elevated to fifth co-founder in 2022, per Moneycontrol - sells up to 2.29 million more, about ₹35 crore.
All four founders, and the finance chief, sell something.
One illustrative transaction holds the whole argument.
A customer places a large fabrication order.
A 2018-vintage Zetwerk would have emailed three factories and invoiced a fee.

The Zetwerk that lists tomorrow signs as the supplier, splits the order across a dozen small plants, finances the working capital, owns the delay if a furnace in Raipur goes down - and books the full order value as revenue.

That is why the top line is ₹15,913 crore and the margins are a contract manufacturer's, why even a year of 40% growth books a loss on the continuing track - ₹81 crore before one-offs, ₹964 crore after them - and why the listing is a question rather than a coronation: has the wrench-holding version of the company finally found the scale where the model's costs stop growing faster than its orders?

What would invalidate the bull case is visible in the same filing: if the managed model's execution costs keep eating the gross margin as revenue scales - if FY27 shows another FY25 - then Zetwerk is a low-margin contractor with a marketplace's valuation story, and the faded grey premium was the honest price all along.

The cash line says the same: operations consumed ₹682 crore in FY26 and another ₹506 crore in the June quarter, and the fresh issue's stated uses are repaying borrowings and acquisitions the company has not yet identified (RHP).
What would confirm it is simpler: a second straight year of growth with the June quarter's continuing-operations loss-narrowing intact.
Tomorrow's open is only the first data point, and the least reliable one.
